children: From agentic AI and precision medicine to connected health data and predictive care, the next phase of healthcare innovation could be defined by technologies that enable more coordinated, personalised and proactive care

Healthcare breakthroughs have historically changed not only how diseases are treated but also how patients experience care. The next major shift may not come from a single drug, device or procedure, but from the convergence of artificial intelligence, genomics, connected health data, robotics and precision medicine.

Artificial intelligence is already moving from experimentation into clinical settings. The US Food and Drug Administration's list of AI-enabled medical devices spans radiology, cardiology, neurology and other specialties. But the next phase could move beyond AI that assists clinicians towards systems that can act within defined workflows.
From AI That Answers To AI That Acts

Healthcare AI has traditionally focused on identifying patterns, supporting diagnosis, assessing risk and assisting decision-making. Agentic AI takes this further by potentially understanding context, breaking objectives into steps, taking defined actions and responding to outcomes. In healthcare, this could include coordinating patient journeys, monitoring clinical information, identifying emerging risks and triggering predefined workflows.

A 2025 WHO assessment covering 50 countries in the European Region found that 32 countries, or 64 per cent, were already using AI-assisted diagnostics, particularly in medical imaging. However, only four had a dedicated national AI strategy for health, while 86 per cent identified legal uncertainty as a major barrier to adoption.

“Agentic AI in healthcare is the tool of the future. It will transform the operating model from AI that answers, to AI that understands context, takes action, learns from outcomes, and remains directionally accountable for clinical and operational workstreams,” says Dr. Sujoy Kar, Chief Medical Information Officer and Senior Vice President, Apollo Hospitals, and former Medical Director, Apollo Gleneagles Hospitals, Kolkata.

The greater the autonomy, however, the greater the need for accountability. Dr. Kar points to Apollo's EASE framework – Ethics, Adoption, Suitability and Explainability – which forms the basis of its 20 Certified Algorithms. “For Agentic AI, EASE framework therefore becomes more consequential, not less,” Dr. Kar says. “The question is no longer simply whether an algorithm predicts correctly, but whether an agent can act safely, recognise uncertainty, hand control back appropriately, learn without compromising clinical governance, and generate measurable benefit at the level of patients, caregivers, and health systems.”

The next healthcare breakthrough is unlikely to belong to AI alone. Genomics and precision medicine are enabling researchers to understand disease at a more individual level. According to the Department of Biotechnology's 2024–25 annual report, GenomeIndia had collected 20,195 samples from 99 communities, with 19,745 available in its biobank.

A stronger India-specific genomic resource could help researchers study disease patterns and treatment responses in a population whose genetic diversity may not always be adequately represented by datasets developed elsewhere. Connected health data adds another layer. As of 31 December 2024, India had created 72.25 crore Ayushman Bharat Health Accounts (ABHAs), with 47.12 crore health records linked to them, according to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

“Tools such as artificial intelligence, remote monitoring, genomics and data-driven decision-making can help doctors detect illnesses earlier and offer more personalised treatment,” says Abhijit CP, Director and Cluster Head – Kolkata and Corporate Growth Initiatives and Hospital Operations, Narayana Health, East. “But technology will make a real difference only when it is accessible, affordable and easy to use in everyday care, including beyond major cities.”

India's e-Sanjeevani platform had facilitated more than 42.66 crore teleconsultations by 31 December 2025, demonstrating the scale at which digital healthcare can extend services beyond conventional hospital settings. “We also need to strengthen preventive healthcare, support our medical professionals and create better-connected systems that allow hospitals, doctors and patients to work together,” Abhijit says.
What Will Define The Next Breakthrough?

The emerging numbers point towards a future where AI, genomics, digital records, remote monitoring and telemedicine increasingly work together rather than operate as isolated technologies. The real measure of innovation may therefore be less about how autonomous a technology is and more about whether it improves care, fits clinical workflows and remains accountable.

Healthcare could be moving from prediction to action, episodic care to continuous intelligence, and generic treatment towards increasingly personalised care. The challenge will be making that transition while preserving human judgement. The next breakthrough may ultimately be the technology that helps doctors see more, act earlier and make better decisions  without losing sight of the patient.
